newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel seen with few options to close budget gap.
newsitem.headline: Waigel seen with few options to close budget gap.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel, fresh from an embarrassing defeat on revaluing Bundesbank reserves, now has almost nowhere to turn to cut Germany's budget deficit in time to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU), analysts said on Thursday.
This is the year that counts for deciding what countries will be in EMU from the January 1999 start.

And with half the year nearly gone, economists said there was not enough time for tax hikes or spending cuts to narrow the budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), even if Waigel could push them through a hostile upper house of parliament.
"In public, the finance minister talks of still getting the budget into shape but the fact is he simply cannot make it," said economist Holger Fahrinkrug at UBS in Frankfurt.
Waigel needs to come up with at least 10 to 15 billion marks ($5.8 to $8.7 billion) in spending cuts or additional revenue if Bonn is to clear the three percent hurdle.
But economists say that at best the government should be able to find four billion marks or so with a spending freeze and one-off measures such as sales of excess oil reserves.
That would still leave Bonn far short of qualifying for EMU and facing a difficult job to secure additional revenues or spending cuts.

Higher taxes are strongly opposed by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition partners, the Free Democrats, and would be likely to result in slower economic growth next year, endangering Germany's ability to achieve a sustainable budget.
"I would not rule out a tax hike but it is unlikely," said Gernot Nerb, economist at Salomon Brothers in Frankfurt.

Even if the FDP were willing to accept higher taxes, it would take several months for any legislation to take effect, meaning the government would only be able to collect revenue for a few months before the end of 1997.
Cuts in social spending, meanwhile, run the same problems as higher taxes -- stiff political opposition and a lack of time to help reduce the deficit.

Although Waigel plans to take in 10 billion marks from the sale of more shares in Deutsche Telekom, proceeds from the move could only be used to help the government reduce its debt ratio, a less-contentious Maastricht target.
"He has missed the point," Fahrinkrug said. "Action should have been taken earlier."
So far Waigel has remained vague about his budget plans and has refused to acknowledge that Germany could fail to meet Maastricht treaty deficit goals.

With few options left, economists said they expected the finance minister to put his hopes in stronger economic growth during the rest of the year that would boost tax revenues and cut unemployment payouts.
Bonn could also get help if state and community budgets, which are counted in national budget calculations for Maastricht, are better than expected.
In the end, however, most now believe that Germany will be forced to try to enter monetary union with a budget deficit of 3.2 percent of GDP or higher.

These are dark days for Waigel. He drew stinging criticism from within his own party and around Europe for a plan to revalue the Bundesbank's official reserves at higher levels and transfer the resulting book profit to Bonn this year.

Although final details of the scheme have not been agreed, Waigel has bowed to stiff pressure from the central bank and has given up transferring profits before 1998 -- too late to help qualify for EMU. ($ = 1.728 German Marks)
